speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, history and contemporaries may judge governments by how they promote cultural development and growth and how they encourage artistic endeavour. Governments come and go, but the artistic achievements, the works of art produced during their mandate remain as witnesses of history.
Although the present Government has not been in power long enough to leave any tangible proof of its support for the arts, it is certainly not on the right track. If the recent cut-backs in federal expenditures on culture are any indication of the Government's intentions, I am convinced that this Government is prepared to preside over a massive erosion of this country's impressive cultural achievements.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps this Government could not care less how it is judged today or in the future on its contribution to the cultural life of this country, but as a Member of this House and as a Canadian citizen, I have no wish to live in a culturally arid climate nor to leave a worthless legacy to future generations. I therefore urge the Government to do everything in its power to enrich our cultural life now and for future generations.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the Government, as I brought to the attention of the former Government about a year ago, the fact that there is a very serious omission in the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, which was amended and passed into law on April 27, 1983.
We are all aware that the amendments, among other things, raised the amount from $20,000 to $60,000 that one could
have on deposit in an account that would be insured against the possibility of a bank, trust company, or other institution in which the funds are deposited, going bankrupt. The Act, as it now reads, applies to funds in savings accounts, and also to fixed deposits for five years or less. However, funds on deposit that are locked in for a period of more than five years are not included and are not protected by the Canada Deposit Insurance Act.
I believe the vast majority of Canadians are unaware of this and believe that their funds are perfectly safe and protected if the term of fixed deposit is more than five years. Therefore, I call upon the Government to make this information readily available to Canadians, and to change the Canada Deposit Insurance Act so that it applies to all deposits, regardless of the number of years during which deposits are in place.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-ACTION PLAN ANNOUNCED BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say few words about the major environmental protection program that will be aimed at reducing acid rain by 50 per cent between now and 1994 and at eliminating more than 45 per cent of hydrocarbon emissions between now and the year 2000.
The action plan announced by the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) is the most ambitious program Canada has ever known. It has no equivalent anywhere in the world.
During the next decade, the offensive against acid rain in Canada will cost the Government more than $300 million. The previous Administration lacked the moral energy and political will to go ahead with such a plan.
In accordance with the strategy that has been announced, the Progressive Conservative Government is going beyond the conventional ecological rhetoric to take concrete action. Incidentally, this decision is part of an on-going process of co-operation with the provinces and especially with industry.
In view of the extent of the damage caused by acid rain, our Government has acknowledged its responsibility for the future of this country and has decided to take action to protect the health, well-being and economic heritage of present and future generations of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, Canada, a medium-sized nation, by giving concrete proof of its desire to take action in this area, was able to convince the President of the United States, who has acknowledged that acid rain is a joint problem for which joint solutions are necessary.

These artists and arts groups are not only fighting against arts cut-backs, but for better, adequate, above poverty level funding for the arts.
The arts community have convinced Canadian public opinion not only of the justice of their cause but of its practicality. Expenditure in the arts means jobs for Canadians and business opportunities for small businesses, especially in tourism. It is
March 20, 1985

healthy for the Canadian economy, as well as being absolutely vital for the Canadian soul.

subsubtopic: BANK OF CANADA ANNUAL REPORT-CONTROL OF PUBLIC EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the long run effect of deficits can be a major obstacle to economic and financial stability. That verdict, given yesterday by Gerald Bouey in his annual report as Governor of the Bank of Canada, may seem like plumbing the depths of the obvious. But it does not seem a bit obvious to the political parties, organizations, and corporations, two of which we have heard from today, that continue to barrage the Government with demands for grants and subsidies. They are still convinced that the Government of Canada has the best credit card in the world, because they think it never has to be paid.
That is why there is a cancer growing in our economic body. It is the cancer of uncontrolled public debt. Only deep therapy can give us the cure, and that is why the House should support government policies that are designed to control expenditure and reduce debt. If Canada does not do that, we will be like passengers on the Titanic, speeding toward the iceberg.

Mr. Speaker, the heart of our cultural and artistic community is being threatened by this insensitive and anti-Canadian Conservative Government. On November 8 last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced reductions in federal spending, the details of which were provided by his colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). The reductions in cultural programs were a major blow to the arts and cultural industries, yet if one examines them closely they have no real impact on the level of over-all spending or on the deficit. In other words, little was made in the way of savings, but a great cost to our cultural life was exacted.
Oral Questions
The arts and the cultural industries are important to Canadian society in terms of their primary role and purpose. They are also important to our economy. To make such small savings at such a great cultural and economic cost is, in my view, false economy of the first order.
The Government must understand that federal support to the arts and the cultural industries is a sound investment, and must begin enhancing that investment now. The arts and the cultural industries are important contributors to Canadian society and the Canadian economy, and merit recognition as such on the part of the Government. I strongly urge the Government to reconsider the reductions and reinstate meaningful levels of support to cultural activity. To do otherwise is to pierce the very heart of our nation.

March 20, 1985
Fisheries Act

The House resumed from Tuesday, March 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fraser that Bill C-32, an Act to amend the Fisheries Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.
Pursuant to the agreement arrived at moments ago, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly).

Mr. Speaker, the important and interesting Bill we are debating today would confer on the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) the absolute and unfettered right to allocate fish without guidelines or restrictions. The Minister thought he always had that right until the court cases last year indicated that the law was deficient and he could not in fact allocate fish. The court went even further and indicated that the Constitution may determine that a law to amend the Fisheries Act to give him the right to allocate fish may be deemed ultra vires.
At present, allocation and the determination of who gets access to the resource is at the heart of the management of the fisheries. During debate on this Bill the Minister has argued in the House and in committee that since he always had that right, the House should automatically give him that right again. I suggest that no legislature should give any Minister this kind of almost absolute or unfettered power to allocate between groups without some guidelines.
I think the key thing is that even the Party in power in the past has put up many complaints against unregulated or unfettered opportunities of Ministers and the Government to determine the lives of people so drastically. We should clarify that this kind of power to determine who has the access to the money that that resource develops, who will be pushed out of that industry, or whose shares will be diminished or capability impaired, should not be given to the Minister or to the Government without some guidelines. What we would like to establish in this House and what user groups would like to establish is that the Minister should put on the record in writing what those guidelines would be.
There is a second interesting aspect to this Bill. The reason this Bill is being given second reading today is that when we hit an impasse in four days of debate, the Government and the Opposition realized it was not in the continuing interests of the people of Canada to hold up the business of the House of Commons. There were some serious questions and contentious issues to be dealt with. The Minister offered to adjourn debate and move this issue into committee for a period of time so we could examine the contentious issues. They were examined in detail.
The Minister has in his possession a summary of the important issues that would form the guidelines. It is my understanding that he has made a commitment to put something in writing on the guidelines that would form part of the records to determine the process of allocation. That is extremely important. It should not be construed by anyone that this Bill is proceeding for any other reason than that of the Government having acted with reasonably good faith and in a constructive and positive way.
The Government adjourned the debate. It did not use closure. It moved the Bill to committee to discuss the contentious issues. It resolved some of the issues but left the most important ones yet to come. This arrangement would not form a commitment to deal expeditiously with this Bill in committee, or a commitment to deal expeditiously at report stage or at third reading, without having something substantial from the Minister. This should be a very clear message from the Opposition, one that will be reinforced by the other Opposition Party here, namely that second reading is given on the basis that we recognize a constructive move was made.
There are four points that must be resolved, and the user groups essentially agree. First, a guideline must state that user groups currently into the industry must have a place in that industry. This allocation gives no indication of that. They must have an opportunity to earn a living from that resource. This Minister must place on the record that his unfettered right to allocate will not impair their position or remove those user groups from the resource.
Second, there must be a board, an agency, made up of user groups. That board should be representative of user groups accountable to the user groups and would be involved in an advisory and co-management process with the Minister. This move formed part of the election campaign promises of the Conservative Party. It makes absolute sense in the fishing industry. The Minister must make some statement in his guidelines on this particular agency and how he will move toward it.

I think the goodwill with which we approached second reading is something that can be worked on again. Some in this House were reluctant to see that precedent, but we worked in committee through some of the most contentious issues while this House went on conducting the business of the people of Canada. Mr. Speaker, you will recall, I am sure, that the other day when I started to speak in the House I had about a minute of my 10 minutes, so I will assume that I have eight or nine minutes left.
In looking at the impact of what the Government is proposing to do, there are three reasons, in my judgment, why the measures that are being taken are inappropriate. The first reason is that the program has indeed been of some considerable benefit. The program has given home owners an opportunity to upgrade their residences. It has benefited the general desire on the part of everyone for conservation.
There is no evidence that I can see that the program has been abused. The moneys made available, at least under certain parts of the Bill-my colleague from Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) looks at me. If there were abuses, they were on the part of those who provided the service, not on the part of those who received it. I believe the home owners themselves took advantage of the program to the extent that it was available.
The moneys that were made available were taxable. Therefore, not even the full cost must be borne by the treasury of the country. For that reason, initially, I would say that the program makes sense. There are large numbers of people in the country who would take advantage of the program were it to be extended. We as a whole would benefit in the long run from the conservation of depletable energy resources that would naturally flow from their taking advantage of the program.
The second point is that it did create employment. It created employment in a number of small businesses that otherwise would have found themselves in serious difficulty. There is no question in my mind that in some aspects of the program there certainly were abuses by those who provided the service. In the insulation area the work frequently was not up to standards that we would have expected. In some instances not only was
Oil Substitution Act
the Government short-changed, but the individual citizens were short-changed as a result of plain, ordinary, bad workmanship, not a reluctance to live up to the obligations.
Nevertheless, the program did provide employment for a large number of people. It provided employment at a time when employment was desperately needed. I do not think we have got past that stage today. There is still the need for employment opportunities for large numbers of people who could continue to be involved in the provision of services that are compensated for under this program. Keep in mind that we still have close to 1.5 million unemployed.
Taking into account that the normal employers in the country are not employing as many people as they did in the past, it would make more sense, in my judgment, to continue to fund this program from the employment point of view rather than to have those people on unemployment insurance, which could well be the case. If you take into account that many of the people who will not be employed as a result of terminating the program may well end up unable to find alternative employment, and if that is true, they will end up on unemployment insurance temporarily and perhaps ultimately on some other form of social program. There is very little benefit derived by society as a whole from forcing that kind of end result.
My judgment would be that from the point of view of maintaining opportunities for employment, this program ought to be at least extended, if not kept in place permanently. I would be prepared to concede that it might not be necessary to keep it in place permanently. There would come a time in the not too distant future where the number of citizens or families who would like to take advantage of it would be small. As more people use it, the need would become less and less. Ultimately the program would come to an end in itself. It comes to an end simply by virtue of the way in which it is structured. Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the House today would postpone consideration of this Bill for six months. I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on this amendment, and I believe my constituents in Bourassa will understand the consequences of this motion. Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that CHIP, the Canadian Home Insulation Program and COSP, the Canadian Oil Substitution Program, were introduced between 1973 and 1977. Perhaps we should recall what the situation was in 1973 to fully understand the gravity of the economic problems that heating costs were creating for Canadians at that time.
The price of oil was increasing quite rapidly, and at the time, most Canadian homes had oil heating, so that heating bills were becoming a problem.
Mr. Speaker, being a truly responsible Government, we thought it would be a good thing to persuade Canadians to upgrade the insulation in their homes and to substitute for oil other forms of energy such as gas, electric power and wood, which have become very popular for home heating. CHIP, the program referred to in Bill C-24, was used to give grants to home owners who were taking steps to conserve energy. [English]
The decision of the Government to abolish this program is not very easy to take. It may be right to say that Canadians must now take up their responsibilities and should insulate or change from oil to other sources of energy themselves if they so wish. I feel that a part of our obligation as parliamentarians is to tell Canadians how we see problems and issues and how better to deal with them.
There are two good programs in place which benefit ordinary Canadians, particularly those of low and middle income. Of the nearly five million residences that were targeted to use the insulation program, only about 2.5 million have done so. Other home owners have indicated an interest in proceeding with these programs after having heard from neighbours how well they work. These programs are primarily aimed at saving oil and thereby heating costs.

Mr. Speaker, this Government has now decided to do away with these two programs. It has the right to do so, since it is in power, but that does not mean I agree with its decision, and I think many Canadians do not agree either, because eliminating these two programs will cause problems for a number of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to elaborate too much on this point, but it would be a good thing if the Government could extend these programs at least until September 30, 1985, so that many contractors and consumers who have already applied for a grant under the program to convert their heating systems can take advantage of the program, and this would also help Canadians to save money. We have had a long, hard winter. Many Canadians have not had a chance to carry out this conversion. We suggest that the Government give these people a chance to take care of this during the spring and summer months.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I simply wish to say that we in the Official Opposition strongly urge the Government to reflect on the advantages of extending these two programs, which I think would be worthwhile for many Canadians.

Deciding in November to axe a program in March, when the program involves home renovation, does not make sense. Everybody knows that not many Canadians are going to do any major changes in their homes in the middle of winter, especially if those changes involve converting the heating system. I am sure that in my hon. friend's riding, people do not change their heating systems in the

middle of a February snow storm. That is why the March 31 date, selected only to do for the benefit of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), makes no sense at all.
This program was quite successful and could have done a lot more good, but unfortunately we now find out that it will be terminated. Mr. Speaker, the Bill before us today illustrates an interesting characteristic of the present Government. The Government, with its overwhelming majority, is one that believes in restraint.
While I believe everyone agrees with restraint, there are different ways to implement restraint. There is sensible restraint, which has several interesting aspects. A Government that would implement sensible restraint would decide on the relevance and efficiency of a program. If it did not meet those requirements, it would be phased out and the resources allocated to that program could be saved and possibly allocated to other programs. That is an example of sensible restraint that has been practised by NDP Government in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia.
Another aspect to carrying out sensible restraint would be to make a small investment in order to rearrange an expensive program. This would ultimately save much more money. For example, investing a relatively small amount in trying to prevent a disease rather than spending much more in finding its cure would ultimately save money. In the past, Governments have invested in a program in order to reap larger benefits later on. The Canadian Oil Substitution Program is one such example. Due to the fact that oil was becomimg too expensive and was having negative effects on the economy, the Government made a small investment so that Canadians would ultimately benefit from a restraint program, but it required that initial investment by the Government.
The same situation applies to the Canadian Home Insulation Program. That small investment by the Government reduces the need for energy consumption, which means that this reasonable and relatively small investment ultimately gives a large return.

Is the House ready for the question? The question is as follows: Miss Carney, seconded by Mrs. Champagne (Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot), moved that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and the Canadian Home Insulation Program Act, be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
Mr. Cassidy, seconded by Mr. Manly, moved in amendment thereto:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Oil Substitution and Conservation Act and
the Canadian Home Insulation Program Act, be not now read a second time
but that it be read a second time this day six months hence".
